name: Singapore
tagline: A garden city of gleaming towers and hawker soul.
bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Aug, Sep, Nov and Dec
whenBlurb: Come February to April for the driest, brightest days; time it to Art Week in January or the Grand Prix in autumn, and expect frequent showers year-round.

ourTake.lede: Singapore is best read as a food city with a skyline, not the other way round, spend as much time in a Tiong Bahru coffee shop as at Marina Bay. The Gardens by the Bay light show is worth it, but go into the Cloud Forest dome at opening before the tour groups. Everyone rushes the Sands SkyPark; the better view is a drink at a bar across the water looking at it.
ourTake.comeIf: You want a spotless, effortless city that families and first-timers navigate without friction.
ourTake.skipIf: You are looking for wilderness, spontaneity or a bargain.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Raffles Hotel Singapore
credentials: World's 50 Best Hotels 2025 (No. 5, highest in Singapore)
items.description: The white colonial grande dame the whole city is measured against, and still the finest room in it.

items.name: Capella Singapore
items.description: A Norman Foster-restored colonial estate in the rainforest, resort calm, minutes from the city.

items.name: The Fullerton Bay Hotel Singapore
items.description: A glass pavilion on the water, looking straight across the bay to the skyline.

items.name: The Paiza Collection at Marina Bay Sands
items.description: The private hotel-within-the-hotel at Marina Bay Sands, arrival by Rolls-Royce, a dedicated lift, total discretion.

items.name: Raffles Sentosa Singapore
items.description: Raffles' all-villa resort debut, private pools and hilltop calm, the marque's newest Singapore address.

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel Singapore
items.description: The surest hands off Orchard Road, quiet, art-filled, and effortless with families.

items.name: Mandarin Oriental, Singapore
items.description: A fan-shaped tower with the group's quiet precision and rooms that fan out over the bay.

items.name: The Ritz-Carlton, Millenia Singapore
items.description: A serious art collection and octagonal-window bathtubs framing the bay, grand, and quietly famous for it.

items.name: The St. Regis Singapore
items.description: Old-world St. Regis grandeur off Orchard, butler service and a museum's worth of art in the halls.

items.name: Conrad Singapore Orchard
items.description: A polished, freshly reimagined Orchard tower, central, capable, and easy on the shopper.

items.name: Marina Bay Sands
items.description: The three-towered icon crowned by the ship-shaped SkyPark, the photograph the whole world knows.

items.name: Conrad Centennial Singapore
items.description: A dependable, art-hung tower by the convention halls, spacious and unshowy.

items.name: Artyzen Singapore
items.description: A calm, design-led newcomer off Orchard, vertical greenery and quiet good taste.

items.name: PARKROYAL COLLECTION Pickering
items.description: The famous hotel-in-a-garden, cascading sky terraces of greenery over the old town.

items.name: The Fullerton Hotel Singapore
items.description: The grand old General Post Office, a neoclassical landmark reborn at the mouth of the river.

items.name: The Capitol Kempinski Hotel Singapore
items.description: Two restored 1930s landmarks turned into a small, characterful house in the civic heart.

items.name: InterContinental Singapore
items.description: Peranakan shophouse charm woven into a grand hotel, over the arts-and-heritage quarter.

items.name: Pan Pacific Singapore
items.description: A soaring atrium tower with wide bay views and a smooth, Asian-service ease.

items.name: Fairmont Singapore
items.description: A big, capable twin-tower house with one of the city's best spas attached.

items.name: Goodwood Park Hotel
items.description: A garden-set heritage landmark of 1900, long a favourite for its quiet lawns and durian pastries.

items.name: W Singapore, Sentosa Cove
items.description: A high-energy design resort by the marina, for members who want the music turned up.

items.name: Gardens by the Bay
credentials: Guinness World Record, Flower Dome, largest glass greenhouse
items.description: The Supertree Grove, the Cloud Forest with the world's tallest indoor waterfall, and the record-holding Flower Dome, a garden built like a city. Come at dusk to walk the OCBC Skyway between the Supertrees, then stay for the free Garden Rhapsody light-and-sound show at night. Wide, flat and pram-friendly, so it works well for a multi-generation group.

items.name: Marina Bay Sands SkyPark Observation Deck
items.description: The ship-shaped deck cantilevered 57 storeys up gives the definitive Singapore skyline view, the bay, the CBD towers and Gardens by the Bay laid out below. Go at golden hour; if you are staying at the hotel you get the famous 150m infinity pool, which non-guests cannot access.

items.name: Singapore Botanic Gardens & National Orchid Garden
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Singapore Botanic Gardens
items.description: Singapore's only UNESCO World Heritage Site and the world's first tropical botanic garden on the list, 82 hectares of rainforest, lakes and heritage trees in the middle of the city. The ticketed National Orchid Garden holds 1,000+ species, including the hybrids named for visiting heads of state. Free entry to the wider gardens; ideal for an unhurried morning walk.

items.name: ArtScience Museum
items.description: The lotus-shaped building beside Marina Bay Sands, best known for the permanent teamLab 'Future World' immersive digital installations that children and adults get equally lost in. It also runs serious travelling exhibitions on science, design and art.

items.name: National Gallery Singapore
items.description: The world's largest public collection of modern Southeast Asian art, housed in the beautifully restored former Supreme Court and City Hall. Worth it for the architecture alone; finish with a drink at the rooftop bar for a Padang-and-bay view. Strong for collectors and anyone who wants depth beyond the theme parks.

items.name: Merlion Park & the Marina Bay waterfront promenade
items.description: The half-lion, half-fish icon spouting water into the bay, with the classic straight-on view of Marina Bay Sands across the water. The best move is simply to walk the full bayfront loop, Merlion to Esplanade to the Helix Bridge to Sands, especially after dark when everything is lit.

items.name: Chinatown & Sri Mariamman Temple / Buddha Tooth Relic Temple
items.description: Restored shophouse lanes, the ornate Sri Mariamman (Singapore's oldest Hindu temple) and the grand red-and-gold Buddha Tooth Relic Temple within a few streets of each other. Wander Pagoda and Temple Streets, then eat at Chinatown Complex or Maxwell. Plenty of vegetarian and South Indian food nearby, which helps veg and Jain travellers.

items.name: Maxwell Food Centre
items.description: The most decorated hawker centre in the city, eight stalls landed in the 2025 Michelin Bib Gourmand list. Home of the legendary Tian Tian Hainanese chicken rice; go early, eat like a local, and understand why Singaporeans take food this seriously.

items.name: Kampong Glam & Sultan Mosque
items.description: The old Malay-Arab quarter, the golden-domed Sultan Mosque, textile and perfume shops on Arab Street, and Haji Lane, a narrow alley of boutiques, murals and rooftop bars. The most atmospheric quarter to wander on foot in the late afternoon.

items.name: Little India & Sri Veeramakaliamman Temple
items.description: The most sensory neighbourhood in Singapore, garland stalls, spice shops, the colourful Tan Teng Niah house and the vivid Sri Veeramakaliamman Temple. For Indian travellers it is both familiar and a revelation; some of the best vegetarian thalis and dosas in the city are here, and Tekka Centre downstairs is a proper wet-market-plus-hawker experience.

items.name: Universal Studios Singapore
items.description: Southeast Asia's Universal park, with zones themed to Jurassic World, Transformers, Sci-Fi City and more, the anchor family attraction on Sentosa. Book Express passes to skip the queues; combine with a Sentosa hotel night to avoid a rushed day.

items.name: S.E.A. Aquarium (Singapore Oceanarium)
items.description: One of the world's largest aquariums, with a vast Open Ocean tank you can sit in front of like a cinema, home to manta rays and sharks. Reliable, air-conditioned and genuinely calming, an easy win with young children or grandparents.

items.name: Night Safari
items.description: The world's first nocturnal wildlife park, you ride a tram through dimly lit habitats to see lions, tapirs and Asian elephants active after dark. A distinctive Singapore evening; opens at 6:30pm, so pair it with the neighbouring parks earlier in the day.

items.name: Singapore Zoo & River Wonders
items.description: Consistently rated among the world's best zoos for its open, moated 'rainforest' design, famous for the Breakfast with Orangutans experience. Adjoining River Wonders adds giant pandas and a huge freshwater collection. The strongest single day out for families with children.

items.name: Bird Paradise
items.description: Asia's largest bird park, with eight walk-through aviaries you can stroll through as free-flying birds swoop around you, and 3,500 birds across 400 species. The newest of the Mandai parks and beautifully designed, quieter and more contemplative than the zoo.

items.name: Tiong Bahru
items.description: Singapore's oldest housing estate, curved 1930s Art Deco blocks, an indie bookshop, third-wave cafés and the excellent Tiong Bahru Market for hawker breakfast. The city's most walkable, low-key morning: no ticket, just wander and eat.

items.name: Katong & Joo Chiat
credentials: UNESCO Asia-Pacific Heritage Award, Joo Chiat conservation
items.description: The heart of Peranakan Singapore, rows of pastel shophouses with ornate ceramic tiles, and the celebrated Koon Seng Road terraces. Come for laksa and kaya toast, and to see a heritage quarter that won a UNESCO Asia-Pacific conservation award. Off the tourist trail and all the better for it.

items.name: Peranakan Museum
items.description: A jewel-box museum devoted to Straits-Chinese culture, beadwork, porcelain, jewellery and the material world of the Peranakans, recently reopened after a full revamp. The best primer before wandering Katong or Emerald Hill.

items.name: National Museum of Singapore
items.description: The country's oldest museum, telling the Singapore story from its trading-port origins through independence, in a grand colonial building with a striking glass rotunda. A good orientation on day one, note the History Gallery is under restoration until late 2026, but the rest remains open.

items.name: The Southern Ridges, Henderson Waves
items.description: A 9km chain of hilltop parks linked by walkways, crowned by Henderson Waves, Singapore's highest pedestrian bridge, a sculptural timber wave 36m up with harbour and skyline views. Do the shorter Mount Faber to HortPark stretch for the best of it; the bridge is lit at night.

items.name: MacRitchie Reservoir & TreeTop Walk
items.description: The city's green lung, boardwalks over the reservoir, monkeys and monitor lizards, and a 250m suspension bridge strung through the rainforest canopy. A proper jungle hike ten minutes from downtown; go early to beat the heat.

items.name: Fort Canning Park
items.description: A hilltop park layered with history, 14th-century royal grounds, WWII bunkers and the famous 'Tree Tunnel' spiral staircase that fills every Instagram feed. A shaded, central green break between museum visits.

items.name: Emerald Hill
items.description: A single, quiet cul-de-sac of exquisitely preserved Peranakan terrace houses tucked just off the Orchard Road shopping strip, a five-minute detour that most visitors miss. Have a drink at one of the old shophouse bars at the foot of the hill.

items.name: Orchard Road
items.description: Singapore's mile of malls, ION Orchard, Ngee Ann City / Takashimaya and Paragon carry the full luxury roster. Efficient, air-conditioned and comprehensive; the practical choice when you want the brands under one roof rather than a hunt.

items.name: The Shoppes at Marina Bay Sands
items.description: The waterfront luxury mall with 170+ premium brands, a canal you can ride a sampan on, and the Apple 'floating' store on the bay. High-end flagship shopping with the Sands spectacle attached, and a rain-proof link to the museum, casino and hotel.

items.name: Raffles Hotel & the Long Bar
items.description: The grand colonial hotel where the Singapore Sling was invented in 1915, restored to full lustre, with an arcade of luxury boutiques and the Long Bar where you still drop peanut shells on the floor. Worth a walk-through and a cocktail even if you are not staying.

items.name: Chijmes
items.description: A restored 19th-century convent and Gothic chapel turned into a courtyard of restaurants and bars, one of the prettiest places in the city for a candlelit dinner. A polished, atmospheric evening away from the malls.

items.name: Clarke Quay & the Singapore River
items.description: The riverside strip of old godowns (warehouses) now full of restaurants and bars, and the departure point for the classic bumboat river cruise past the Merlion to Marina Bay. Do the cruise at dusk for the city lights; the nightlife here has just been refreshed.

items.name: Lau Pa Sat
items.description: A gorgeous Victorian cast-iron market hall, a national monument, packed with hawker stalls, where the neighbouring street closes each evening to become the smoky 'Satay Street'. The most convenient CBD hawker experience and a beautiful building in its own right.

items.name: Chinatown Complex Market & Food Centre
items.description: Singapore's largest hawker hub, 700+ stalls over several floors, including the stall that once held a Michelin star for soya-sauce chicken. Gritty, authentic and endlessly cheap; go with an empty stomach and no plan.

items.name: Haw Par Villa
items.description: A gloriously eccentric 1930s park of lurid dioramas illustrating Chinese mythology, most famously the graphic 'Ten Courts of Hell'. Free, strange and unforgettable; nothing else in the city is remotely like it.

items.name: Sri Mariamman Temple
items.description: Singapore's oldest Hindu temple, its rainbow gopuram tower crowded with painted deities rising incongruously out of Chinatown. During the annual Theemithi festival, devotees walk over hot coals in the courtyard. A moving, active place of worship, for Indian travellers, a piece of home in an unexpected setting.

items.name: Thian Hock Keng Temple
items.description: The city's oldest and most important Hokkien temple, built in 1839 by grateful immigrants where the sea once lapped the shore, an exquisite piece of southern-Chinese architecture on Telok Ayer Street. Pair it with the mosque and church on the same historic street of faiths.

items.name: Singapore Flyer
items.description: The giant observation wheel over the bay, with 30-minute rotations that reveal the skyline, the Formula 1 street circuit and, on a clear day, Malaysia and Indonesia. You can book a private capsule with dinner for a discreet celebration.

items.name: Jewel Changi Airport & the HSBC Rain Vortex
items.description: The world's tallest indoor waterfall thundering seven storeys through a glass dome ringed by rainforest, and it is inside the airport. Worth a deliberate visit even without a flight; a genuinely jaw-dropping arrival or departure, and a fine last few hours before you fly.

items.name: Pulau Ubin
items.description: A 15-minute bumboat from Changi Point drops you into Singapore of the 1960s, a rustic island of last-remaining kampong (village) life, mangroves and jungle you explore by rented bicycle. The Chek Jawa wetlands at low tide are extraordinary. The city's easiest escape into another era.

items.name: Palawan Beach & the Southern Ridges of Sentosa
items.description: Sentosa's family beach, with a rope suspension bridge out to the 'Southernmost Point of Continental Asia' and a lookout tower. Low-key, shaded and easy, a gentler counterpoint to the island's theme parks.

items.name: Esplanade, Theatres on the Bay
items.description: The 'durian'-domed performing arts centre on the bayfront, world-class concerts, theatre and a strong run of free performances on the outdoor stage most evenings. Check the programme; there is nearly always something on, much of it free.

items.name: Singapore Cable Car (Mount Faber to Sentosa)
items.description: A glass cabin gliding from a rainforest hilltop across the harbour to Sentosa, with the port, container ships and Southern Islands spread below. The most scenic way to reach the island; private-cabin dining is available for a special occasion.

items.name: Gillman Barracks
items.description: A cluster of restored 1930s colonial army barracks turned contemporary-art enclave, commercial galleries, artist studios and a relaxed café or two under old rain trees. The quiet, serious end of the Singapore art scene, and pleasantly uncrowded.

items.name: Fort Siloso
items.description: Singapore's only preserved coastal fort, with WWII gun emplacements and tunnels and a treetop 'Skywalk' out to the ramparts. A substantial, breezy history stop on Sentosa that balances out the theme-park day.

items.name: Coney Island (Pulau Serangoon)
items.description: A rugged, deliberately undeveloped nature park on the northeast coast, coastal forest, casuarina groves and quiet beaches, best explored on foot or by bike. One of the last genuinely wild-feeling corners of Singapore, and rarely busy.

items.name: Bintan Island day trip (Indonesia)
items.description: A one-hour ferry from Tanah Merah reaches Bintan's beach resorts and spas, the standard Singapore beach escape for a day or an overnight. A useful reset when the city gets intense; passport and visa-on-arrival apply, so plan the paperwork.

items.name: Johor Bahru & Legoland day trip (Malaysia)
items.description: Across the causeway lies Malaysia, cheaper spa days, seafood, and Legoland Malaysia for younger children, all doable as a day trip. Weekday mornings avoid the border crush; keep passports handy.

items.name: Marina Barrage
items.description: A dam-turned-park with a grassy rooftop that is the city's favourite kite-flying and sunset picnic spot, and a rare uncrowded, front-row view straight across the water to the Marina Bay skyline. Quietly one of the best free things to do at dusk.

items.name: Kranji countryside & Sungei Buloh Wetland Reserve
credentials: ASEAN Heritage Park, Sungei Buloh Wetland Reserve
items.description: The rural far northwest, mangrove boardwalks alive with migratory birds, mudskippers and the occasional estuarine crocodile, plus a scatter of hydroponic and goat farms. An unexpectedly wild, agricultural side of Singapore that almost no visitor sees.

items.name: Odette
items.description: Julien Royer's modern French inside the National Gallery, the city's most decorated table.

items.name: Les Amis
items.description: A French institution since 1994, classical haute cuisine and one of Asia's great cellars.

items.name: Zén
items.description: Björn Frantzén's Singapore house, Scandinavian purity meets Japanese finesse across three floors of a shophouse.

items.name: Cloudstreet
items.description: Rishi Naleendra's precise, fermentation-led cooking, Sri Lankan soul, exacting technique.

items.name: Jaan by Kirk Westaway
items.description: 'Reinventing British' cooking on the 70th floor, technique and a view in equal measure.

items.name: Meta
items.description: Sun Kim's highwire act between Korea and Europe, inventive, assured, quietly thrilling.

items.name: Saint Pierre
items.description: Emmanuel Stroobant's French-Asian cooking, waterside, with the bay for a backdrop.

items.name: Shoukouwa
items.description: An eight-seat sushi counter flown daily from Toyosu, the quietest luxury in town.

items.name: Thevar
items.description: Spice-spiked modern Indian cooking that earned Singapore's most exciting two-star climb.

items.name: Sushi Sakuta
items.description: A serene Edomae counter, newly promoted, precise, unhurried, deeply traditional.

items.name: Waku Ghin
items.description: Tetsuya Wakuda's intimate multi-room dinner at Marina Bay Sands, Japanese-European, jewel-like.

items.name: Cut by Wolfgang Puck
items.description: Wolfgang Puck's modern steakhouse, the city's most polished room for a great cut.

items.name: Burnt Ends
items.description: Everything through the custom four-tonne ovens, the barbecue counter that became a pilgrimage.

items.name: Candlenut
items.description: The world's first Michelin-starred Peranakan kitchen, Malcolm Lee's refined Nyonya cooking.

items.name: Labyrinth
items.description: Han Liguang's 'new Singaporean' cooking, hawker memories reimagined with local farms.

items.name: Seroja
items.description: Kevin Wong's ode to Nusantara flavours, Malay-archipelago cooking with real elegance.

items.name: Euphoria
items.description: Jason Tan's 'gastro-botanica', vegetable-led fine dining of great delicacy.

items.name: Summer Pavilion
items.description: Refined Cantonese in a garden-pavilion setting, the grand Chinese lunch, immaculately done.

items.name: Shisen Hanten by Chen Kentaro
items.description: Third-generation Szechuan mastery, mapo tofu the way it should be.

items.name: Iggy's
items.description: A long-running critical darling, European cooking with a wine list to match.

items.name: Nouri
items.description: Ivan Brehm's 'crossroads cooking', a thoughtful blur of world cuisines under one star.

items.name: Nae:um
items.description: Louis Han's memory-led Korean cooking, seasonal, personal, quietly moving.

items.name: Buona Terra
items.description: A warm, family-run Italian doing quietly excellent contemporary cooking.

items.name: Alma by Juan Amador
items.description: European fine dining with a light, generous hand in a garden-hotel setting.

items.name: Summer Palace
items.description: Classic, exacting Cantonese, the grand hotel Chinese dinner at its most assured.

items.name: Imperial Treasure Fine Teochew Cuisine
items.description: Teochew cooking done with rare precision, braised goose and clear, clean flavours.

items.name: Lei Garden
items.description: A Cantonese stalwart in the Chijmes cloisters, dim sum and roast meats, done properly.

items.name: Whitegrass
items.description: Contemporary Australian-French cooking in a restored chapel-precinct room.

items.name: Araya
items.description: A refined Latin-American tasting menu, precise, warm and hard to book.

items.name: Pangium
items.description: Malcolm Lee's second act, Southeast-Asian heritage cooking with a green conscience.

items.name: Kotuwa
items.description: Modern Sri Lankan cooking with real fire and spice, hoppers and curries done with care.

items.name: Jungle
items.description: Bold, herb-driven Thai cooking that punches well above its price.

items.name: Jigger & Pony
items.description: Singapore's best bar, and among Asia's finest, a cocktail room the world flies in for.

items.name: Nutmeg & Clove
items.description: Cocktails that tell Singapore's own story, local flavours, world-class craft.

items.name: Analogue
items.description: A sustainability-minded bar in the Chijmes cloisters, inventive, and quietly conscientious.

items.name: Native
items.description: Regional Southeast-Asian spirits and foraged flavours, a bar with a real sense of place.

items.name: Hill Street Tai Hwa Pork Noodle
items.description: The bak chor mee that holds a Michelin star, proof a single hawker bowl can be world-class.

items.name: Boon Tong Kee
items.description: A legendary Hainanese chicken rice house, freshly promoted for doing the classic best.

items.name: Ji Ji Wanton Noodle Specialist
items.description: A Hong Lim hawker favourite, newly starred by the Bib for its wanton mee.

items.name: Nam Sing Hokkien Fried Mee
items.description: A famed hawker plate of Hokkien mee, smoky, wet, and quietly perfect.

items.name: Sin Heng Claypot Bak Koot Teh
items.description: Peppery pork-rib soup in a claypot, old-Singapore comfort, credentialed by the inspectors.

items.name: To-Ricos Kway Chap
items.description: A beloved kway chap stall, braised, soulful, and worth the queue.

items.name: Song Kee Teochew Fish Porridge
items.description: Clean, restorative Teochew fish porridge, the antidote to a heavy week.

items.name: Lao Fu Zi Fried Kway Teow
items.description: Char kway teow with real wok hei, the smoky char that defines the dish.

items.name: Kitchenman Nasi Lemak
items.description: Fragrant coconut-rice nasi lemak done with a cook's care, a Bib-listed favourite.

items.name: Jigger & Pony
items.description: The city's defining cocktail room, polished, unhurried, and among the best on earth.

items.name: Atlas
credentials: Rémy Martin Legend of the List Award (2024)
items.description: An Art Deco cathedral to gin, a 15-metre tower of 1,300 labels beneath a soaring 1930s ceiling.

items.name: Nutmeg & Clove
items.description: Cocktails that tell Singapore's own story, local flavours, world-class craft.

items.name: Native
items.description: Regional spirits and foraged flavours, a bar with a real, rooted sense of place.

items.name: Sago House
items.description: A hand-built shophouse bar of upcycled charm, six classics, remade weekly from the market.

items.name: Offtrack
items.description: Vinyl on the turntable, pan-Asian plates and drinks, the easy, low-lit end of world-class.

items.name: Cat Bite Club
items.description: An agave den hidden in plain sight, tequila and mezcal handled with real seriousness.

items.name: Analogue
items.description: A sustainability-minded bar in the Chijmes cloisters, inventive, and quietly conscientious.

items.name: Side Door
items.description: A new entrant that arrived straight into the ranks, precise, confident, worth the seat.

items.name: Origin Bar
items.description: A grand-hotel bar with real craft behind it, the polished nightcap done properly.

items.name: Smoke & Mirrors
credentials: Time Out World's 2nd Best Rooftop Bar (2024)
The World's 50 Best Bars Discovery listing
items.description: Above the National Gallery, staring down the Padang to the bay, the city's finest rooftop terrace.

items.name: CÉ LA VI
credentials: Landmark SkyPark rooftop atop Marina Bay Sands; internationally recognised
items.description: Fifty-seven floors up on the SkyPark, the definitive high-above-the-bay drink.

items.name: Lantern
credentials: Landmark bay-level rooftop of The Fullerton Bay Hotel; Forbes Travel Guide 5-Star hotel
items.description: A rooftop pool bar at the water's edge, the softer, quieter front-row seat to the skyline.

items.name: Employees Only
items.description: The New York speakeasy's Singapore outpost, showman bartending and a room that runs late.

plan.heading: 4 days in Singapore, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Cloud Forest and Supertrees of Gardens by the Bay before the heat, unhurried.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Check into the Raffles, high tea in the Grand Lobby, then the National Gallery in the old Supreme Court.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Odette, the three-Michelin room in the same building, booked well ahead.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The shophouses of Chinatown and the temples, then a Peranakan morning in Katong and Joo Chiat.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch of laksa, then the colours of Little India and the perfumers of Kampong Glam.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Burnt Ends or Zén, then cocktails at Atlas in its art-deco tower.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A morning at the Southern Ridges and Henderson Waves, then a boat around the harbour.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch at Sentosa, then the pool and quiet of the Capella on the island's forested edge.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Cure or Meta, and a nightcap watching the container ships from the terrace.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The orchids of the Singapore Botanic Gardens, a UNESCO site, in the cool of the morning.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch at Candlenut, the Michelin Peranakan table, then boutiques along Orchard and Dempsey Hill.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A farewell dinner at Les Amis, then the skyline from the CÉ LA VI rooftop over Marina Bay.

items.name: Marina Bay
items.description: The postcard address, for first-timers who want the icons within walking distance.

items.name: Tiong Bahru
items.description: Art-deco walk-ups, indie cafés and the best local market, suits repeat visitors.

items.name: Sentosa Cove
items.description: Waterfront villas and resorts, for families or a beach-leaning stay.

events.name: Singapore Grand Prix
events.note: The original F1 night race, run through the streets around Marina Bay with headline concerts.

events.name: Chinese New Year
events.note: Chinatown lights up and the Chingay parade fills the streets, the city's biggest celebration.

events.name: Singapore Art Week
events.note: Anchored by ART SG, the region's largest fair, with gallery openings across the island.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Marina Bay suits first-timers who want the skyline; Orchard for shopping, the quieter Dempsey and Sentosa for calm. The city is famously strict, no littering, no chewing gum sales, no jaywalking, and impeccably safe. Book the tasting-menu tables well ahead, as the best fill weeks out.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Land at Changi (SIN), the benchmark of modern airports, where fast immigration and a chauffeured car, or the hotel's own limousine, put you in Marina Bay or Orchard within twenty-five minutes.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: The city is walkable, immaculate and easily covered by private car; the MRT is world-class if you ever wish to move like a local, and Sentosa is a short causeway away.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: An eSIM (Singtel or a global provider) gives instant 5G, though free wifi is everywhere and reliable; connectivity is never a concern here.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: The Singapore dollar (SGD); cards and contactless are near-universal, cash is seldom needed, and tipping is not customary as a service charge is already added.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: February to April is the kindest: drier, less humid, comfortable for a tropical city. It is warm and humid year-round; the November-January northeast monsoon brings the heaviest rain, and June-July can see afternoon showers, though July stays relatively dry.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Direct from Delhi and Mumbai, both around 5.5-6 hours, and from Bengaluru. Singapore Airlines flies it best, with a superb business cabin (and first on select rotations). SilverKris and The Private Room lounges at Changi are among the world's finest, and Changi itself makes onward connections a pleasure rather than a chore.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations required beyond routine; hepatitis A worth having. One of the safest cities in the world, with immaculate public order. Tap water is fully potable straight from the tap. No altitude or water concerns; the only note is heat and humidity.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Excellent for vegetarian and Jain travellers. Little India offers outstanding pure-veg and Jain-friendly dining, and hawker centres and hotels understand the requirements well. Komala Vilas and MTR are dependable South Indian names; fine-dining kitchens prepare Jain readily on notice.
